title: Electron shuttling as a probe for charge defects
authors: Hamza Jnane, Tamas Daniel Lipovics, Guido Burkard
abstract: Silicon spin qubits are a leading platform for scalable quantum computing, but their performance is limited by charge noise, widely attributed to two-level fluctuators (TLFs). The location of individual TLFs is generally unknown, and existing methods to localise them does not scale favourably with device size. Here, we show that electron shuttling turns a single mobile spin into a scanning probe of individual defects. We show that by shuttling a spin over a range of distances and tracking its coherence loss, one can localise defects along the channel and constrain their switching rate and fluctuation amplitude. Because one shuttled electron sweeps an extended region, the approach scales more favourably than previous methods. Our protocol requires no additional hardware and provides a practical route to mapping the charge-defect landscape of large silicon devices, enabling defect-aware calibration and avoidance in shuttling-based architectures.
summary: The paper proposes using controlled electron shuttling in silicon spin qubits to map and characterize charge defects (TLFs). By measuring the resulting loss of spin coherence (infidelity), researchers can localize these noise sources and determine their switching dynamics. This offers a practical, hardware-agnostic method for improving solid-state quantum computing platforms.
main_problem: Charge noise, caused by Two-Level Fluctuators (TLFs), limits the performance of silicon spin qubits for quantum computation.
main_result: Electron shuttling acts as a scalable scanning probe to localize charge defects and characterize their switching rates without requiring additional hardware.
method: The authors analyze the dephasing factor by modeling the time evolution of the spin's coherence during controlled back-and-forth electron shuttling over a defect site.
model_or_system: The system involves single spin qubits in silicon interacting with charge noise modeled by TLFs, whose effect is incorporated into the qubit Hamiltonian via g-factor modulation. The dynamics are solved using coupled differential equations for probability amplitudes.
key_observables: Dephasing factor ($W(T)$) and its derived quantity, the infidelity ($1 - |W(T)|$), which quantifies decoherence due to defects.
important_parameters: The fluctuation regime ($\gamma_T \ll 1$ vs. $\gamma_T \gg 1$) and the shuttling distance $L$ are key parameters used to extract defect properties.
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on approximations, such as expanding exponentials or assuming specific limits for the fluctuation rate relative to the measurement time.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the infidelity versus shuttling distance ($L$) under different fluctuation regimes and show how this dependence allows defect localization. Another figure compares results with varying interface roughness ($	ext{RMS}$).
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework by deriving the evolution of the coherence factor based on the time-dependent g-factor modulation from a TLF, solving the resulting differential equations in different fluctuation limits, and demonstrating defect localization via the measured infidelity.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, scalable measurement protocol for characterizing noise sources (TLFs) that fundamentally limit solid-state quantum memories, directly impacting qubit coherence time predictions.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Illustration of shuttling-based defect probing. An electron is shuttled back and forth in the x-direction. For simplicity, we represent a charge defect fluctuating in the x-direction in red but consider fluctuations in 3D in the main text. The closer the shuttled electron is to the defect (red zone in the potential landscape), the more spin dephasing it experiences. The goal is to leverage this to characterise the average position x0 of the TLF by measuring the average phase the electron has accumulated during its trip. This illustration is inspired by Fig. 2 of [7].

FIG. 2. Infidelity (1 −|W|) in dependence of the shuttling distance L when the TLF is fluctuating in the x-direction for the FB protocol (red). We explore three different regimes: static defect (γT ≪1, left), fast fluctuations (γT ≫1, centre) and intermediate fluctuations (γ = 1 MHz, right). The agreement between the analytically derived results (red line) with Monte-Carlo simulations (crosses) is very good. The mean position of the defect is chosen to be x0 = 500 nm (vertical dashed line). Generally, parameters are chosen according to Table I, with fluctuations in the y- and z-direction equal to zero here. FIG. 3. (Top) Evolution of the infidelity (1 −|W|) as a func- tion of the shuttling distance L along different Si/SiO2 inter- face (RMS) roughness values. The crosses represent results of Monte-Carlo simulations with 105 shots. (Bottom) Physical interface terrain profiles.

FIG. 4. Infidelity with respect to shuttling distance when the TLF is fluctuating in the x-direction. The left panel corresponds to an electron being shuttled back and forth with a 1 µs pause at the turning point (FWB protocol). In the right panel, we study an electron travelling in one direction from x = 0 to x = 1000 nm. The x axis corresponds to the position at which the electron is stopped for 1 µs to accumulate phase before resuming its journey (FWF protocol). The mean position of the defect is chosen to be x0 = 500 nm (vertical dashed line). Generally, parameters are chosen according to Table I.

The mean position of the defect is chosen to be x0 = 500 nm (vertical dashed line). Generally, parameters are chosen according to Table I.
